articles.title: 关于人生观
articles.body:
我是一个普通的人。家里没有很多钱，但不至于吃不饱穿不暖。没有擅长的东西，学的东西都会点但是都不太会。没有特别的爱好，原来以为自己喜欢唱歌，但后来发现也没那么执着。没有抛不下的朋友，所有人都可以是我的朋友，但又好像都不是我的朋友。唯一有的就是我无从选择的家人，对我很好很善良的家人，我一直心怀愧意的家人。

我和所有东西之间都有一层隔阂。这些东西从来都不是我的，对我来说也只是过客，没什么是真正重要的。不管是物品，还是生命。我喜欢动物，喜欢植物，喜欢人类，喜欢自然，但它们也留不住我。我喜欢音乐，喜欢艺术，喜欢美，喜欢娱乐，但它们也留不住我。我的喜欢，对我来说只是消磨时间的方式，实则一文不值。我也没有爱过、恨过、怒过、伤过，我的身上没有过什么特别的情绪波动。就连被突然吓到的反应都是我刻意练习出来的。我厌倦成绩，厌倦攀比，厌倦所谓的上进、成功、梦想、希望。我不是曾经没有过，只是我现在真的对这些只能感到厌恶和恶心。

在这个世界上，我觉得没有什么能留下我。

除了我的父母。

我从小和父母一起生活。过年时回父亲的老家，偶尔回母亲的老家。父亲的老家我更熟悉，那里我认为是我的根。但我的家依旧在有父母的家，只有父母的那个家。父母对我很好，亲戚也对我很好，我很感恩。如果我离开了，父母一定会对辛苦养大的孩子感到伤心。我的离开会让他们怎么想呢。这是我留下的唯一一个原因。我对父母有愧，对亲人有愧。我想感恩他们，但我，也想逃避，只想怀抱着无尽的愧疚感负罪感决然离开。

但我还是为了不要让父母感到伤心而活着。我不敢担负起沉重的愧疚和负罪感。因为他们真的很好。我不希望他们受到伤害，不管是从别人那里来的，还是从我这里带给他们的。

为了继续活下去，我强迫自己相信一件事：我是想活的，不是想死的。如果我的出发点是想死的，我就会想世界上有什么在牵绊着我不能死去。理到最后，发现只有那沉重的愧疚感在牵绊着我。而如果出发点是想活的，我就会想有什么东西是一定要我死的。我很累，我厌倦了这样的日子，我感到空虚，所有的爱好所有的情感都离我而去，这些并不是一定要我死的。唯一一定要我死的情况，可能就是飞来横祸了。有了这个信仰，至少我可以强迫自己活下去。强迫自己相信这个信仰，然后强迫自己活下去，强迫自己面对令人烦躁的一切。

我并不擅长与社会相处。我不是外向的人，不会主动发起话题，不会主动结交他人，我习惯经过长期的相处慢慢建立信任。我不习惯除了公事交谈以外与陌生人搭话，有时说公事前我也要字斟句酌，因为感觉不管怎么说都很尴尬。我不擅长自我介绍，我不知道能说什么。我能说的只有简历上寥寥的几笔，不能说的也不需要说的可太多了。真要介绍，得像是这样长篇大论的介绍才算真实彻底，那些场面话对我来说就是逢场作戏，扮演我在社会中的良好形象罢了，这让我作呕。也许别人不觉得有什么，反而乐在其中，但我只会感到恶心。可是，这样冗长乏味的自我介绍，又有几个人愿意听呢。

大家只想听到那个戴着面具的人的角色设定而已。是真是假都没有那么重要。骗别人一辈子，就一辈子都是那样了。

但我不喜欢那样。不喜欢就是理由。

可是很多时候，我不得不那样。我早已在过去的生活中把自己规训成了那样，这个角色我还要继续扮演下去，也许直到尽头，也许马上就可以抛开这些。我也不知道。生活一直在继续，疯狂啃噬着我的时间和身体，我没有余力去思考这么多，只能遵循熟悉的规则去敷衍度日。当一个人躺在床上面对黑暗的时候，才能抽身去思考、去记录，然后像死去般昏睡，为下一天的痛苦做好准备。

我会预设所有人都对我怀有恶意。父母出去办事过了预计的时间我就会开始焦躁，疯狂担心是不是被车撞到了，被人重伤了，跌倒了爬不起来了，过了几小时给我打一个电话问我是不是 xxx 的家属，诸如此类。坐地铁会担心地铁故障，坐网约车会担心司机有问题，坐自家车会担心车祸桥塌爆炸，躺在床上会担心入室火灾毒气地震海啸。为了正常生活下去，我强迫自己相信第二条信仰：坏人没有那么多。不会有那么多天灾人祸，就算地铁停运也会有人马上过来修好的。这有效提升了我对社会运行的信任度，签合同的时候我能强迫自己安心对方应该不会跑路，小组作业的时候我能强迫自己安心把一部分工作交给其他人，过马路时我能强迫自己接受大概率应该不会有车朝我冲过来。我依然无法无条件信任他人，但我会强迫自己无条件相信我的信仰，即使冒出被害妄想的念头也能强迫自己去多信任一些。

第一个信仰也是这样，如果不强迫自己去相信，我很难活下去。

我的离去对世界来说什么也不是。我的存在也是。我不明白为什么我要为了活下去而不得不活成半死不活的样子。我暂时还没有想到第三条信仰能够帮我回答这个问题。

信仰对我来说是解药。它们能让很多事情变得简单，能让纷乱的思绪安静下来。但当遇到信仰无法解决的事情，我就只能寻找新的信仰。我活在我给自己打造的规则怪谈里，每一条规则我必须无条件服从，否则就会遭殃。同时作为规则怪谈的管理者，遇到会遭殃的情况，还要不断想出新的规则来帮我应付过去。信仰也是让人上瘾的毒药，只是至少在当下，能切实地让我轻松一些，逃避一些。

关于我自己的介绍到这里已经足够多了。

也许没有人会看到这里。

再见。
articles.bodyEn:
I'm an ordinary person. My family doesn't have much money, but we never went hungry or went cold. I have nothing I'm good at — I've picked up a little of everything and mastered none of it. I have no real passion. I once thought I loved singing, but later found I wasn't so attached to it after all. There is no friend I couldn't let go of. Anyone can be my friend, and yet somehow no one really is. The only thing I truly have is the family I never got to choose — a family that has been kind and good to me, a family I have always carried a debt of guilt toward.

There is a distance between me and everything. None of it was ever mine. To me it's all just passing through; nothing is truly important. Objects, or living things. I like animals, I like plants, I like people, I like nature — but none of them can hold me here. I like music, I like art, I like beauty, I like entertainment — but none of them can hold me here either. The things I like are only ways to pass the time. Truthfully, they're worth nothing. I have never loved, never hated, never raged, never been wounded. No remarkable emotion has ever moved through me. Even the way I react when I'm startled is something I deliberately practiced. I'm weary of grades, weary of comparison, weary of so-called ambition and success and dreams and hope. It's not that I never had them. It's that now, these words only make me feel disgust and nausea.

In this world, I don't think there is anything that could keep me here.

Except my parents.

I grew up living with my parents. At New Year we'd go back to my father's hometown, and occasionally to my mother's. My father's hometown is the one I know better — that's where I think my roots are. But home is still wherever my parents are. Only the home with my parents in it. My parents are very good to me, and so are my relatives. I'm grateful. If I left, my parents would surely grieve for the child they worked so hard to raise. What would my leaving make them feel? That is the one reason I stay. I feel guilty toward my parents, guilty toward my family. I want to repay them. But I also want to run away — to turn and leave decisively, cradling an endless burden of guilt and blame.

And still, I live so that my parents won't be hurt. I don't dare take on the weight of that guilt. Because they really are good people. I don't want them to be wounded — not by others, and not by me.

To keep going, I force myself to believe one thing: I want to live, not to die. If I start from wanting to die, I begin asking what in this world is holding me back from dying. And when I trace it to the end, I find only that heavy guilt holding me. But if I start from wanting to live, I ask instead what would make it necessary for me to die. I'm tired. I'm exhausted by living this way. I feel empty. Every interest and every feeling has left me — but none of that makes death necessary. The only thing that would truly require me to die is a freak accident. With this belief, at least I can force myself to go on living. Force myself to believe it, then force myself to keep living, force myself to face everything that irritates and exhausts me.

I'm not good at being in society. I'm not an extrovert. I don't start conversations, I don't reach out to people. I'm used to building trust slowly, through long stretches of time together. I'm not used to speaking with strangers about anything other than business, and even before I say something businesslike I weigh every word, because it feels awkward no matter how I put it. I'm bad at introducing myself. I don't know what to say. All I can offer are the few sparse lines on a résumé; there is far too much I can't say and don't need to say. To introduce myself honestly would take something long-winded like this — only that would be real and complete. The pleasantries are just playing a part, acting out my presentable image in society. It makes me sick. Maybe others don't mind; maybe they even enjoy it. But all I feel is nausea. And yet — how many people would be willing to sit through an introduction this long and tedious?

People only want to hear the character settings of the person behind the mask. Whether it's true or not doesn't matter much. Lie to others for a lifetime, and that becomes who you are for a lifetime.

But I don't like that. Not liking it is reason enough.

But much of the time, I have no choice but to do it. Somewhere in the life I've already lived, I disciplined myself into being that way, and I have to go on playing this role — maybe until the very end, maybe I'll be able to cast it all off any minute now. I don't know which. Life just keeps going, gnawing frantically at my time and my body. I have no strength left over to think this much. All I can do is follow the familiar rules and muddle through the days. It's only when I'm lying in bed, facing the dark, that I can step out of it — to think, to write things down — and then fall asleep as if dead, getting ready for the next day's pain.

I assume everyone wishes me harm. When my parents go out and stay past the time they said they'd be back, I start to panic, frantically worrying whether they've been hit by a car, badly hurt by someone, or have fallen and can't get up — that in a few hours the phone will ring and someone will ask if I'm the family of so-and-so. On the subway I worry about breakdowns. In a rideshare I worry about the driver. In our own car I worry about crashes, collapsing bridges, explosions. Lying in bed I worry about a fire, gas, an earthquake, a tsunami. In order to live normally, I force myself to believe a second creed: there aren't that many bad people. There won't be that many disasters. Even if the subway stops, someone will come fix it right away. This has measurably raised my trust in how society runs. Signing a contract, I can force myself to believe the other party probably won't run off with the money. In group work, I can force myself to hand part of the task to someone else. Crossing the street, I can force myself to accept that most likely no car will come charging at me. I still cannot trust people unconditionally. But I can force myself to believe my creed unconditionally — and even when paranoid thoughts surface, force myself to trust a little more.

The first creed works the same way. If I don't force myself to believe it, it's hard to stay alive.

My leaving would mean nothing to the world. Neither does my being here. I don't understand why I have to live half-dead just in order to go on living. I haven't yet thought of a third creed that could answer that question for me.

Creeds are my medicine. They simplify a great many things; they quiet the noise in my head. But when I meet something a creed can't solve, I can only go looking for a new one. I live inside a rules-horror story I built for myself, where every rule must be obeyed without condition or something bad will happen. And as the administrator of that story, whenever I run into a situation where something bad will happen, I have to keep inventing new rules to get myself through it. Creeds are also an addictive poison. It's just that, for now at least, they genuinely make things lighter, and let me escape a little.

That's enough about me.

Maybe no one will read this far.

Goodbye.
